- deep learning progress over last decade enabled by massive, high-quality datasets
- real annotated datasets: noisy labels, from annotation scheme biases (cite) or inherent ambiguity (cite)
- challenge: avoid overfitting noisy data, robust generalization
- large models: memorization and generalization can coexist (cite)
- tussle between the two, esp. with label corruption, poorly understood

2. Generative LMs
- memorization more nuanced
- some factual knowledge needed for accurate info
- verbatim memorization of training data unwanted: privacy (cite)
- conditions affecting memorization in LLMs still under investigation (cite)
- larger models and repeated data (cite) favor memorization

steps.text:
Deep learning has made astounding progress in the last decade, and this has been helped by massive, high-quality datasets. Real-world datasets that are annotated will always contain noisy labels, because of biases of annotation schemes or because of inherent ambiguity. So a key challenge when training large models is to not overfit the noisy data and to get robust generalization. But in large models, memorization and generalization can also coexist. Overall, the tussle between memorization and generalization, especially when labels are corrupted, is still poorly understood.

For generative language models the memorization problem is even more nuanced. Some factual knowledge is critical so that the language models give accurate information. But verbatim memorization of the training data is generally not wanted because of privacy concerns. What conditions affect memorization in large language models (LLMs) is still being investigated. In particular, larger models and repeated data favor memorization.

In this work we try to disentangle generalization and memorization with an approach motivated by theoretical physics. That is, we focus on simple models that are analytically tractable and ("mechanistically") interpretable, trained on algorithmic datasets. More concretely, we study two-layer Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) that are trained on modular arithmetic tasks. Here the network is trained to learn a rule, such as z=(m+n)\%p\equiv m+n\,\,\textrm{mod}\,\,p from a number of examples, and the tasks are phrased as classification problems. Then we force the network to memorize \xi\cdot 100\% of the examples by corrupting the labels, i.e. we inject data points where (m+n)\%p is mapped to z^{\prime}\neq z. In this setting the generalizing representations are understood qualitatively and also quantitatively, because an analytic solution for the representations is available, described in previous work. We show empirically that networks that are large enough can memorize the corrupted examples and still get nearly perfect generalization on the test set. We can identify the neurons responsible for memorization using inverse participation ratio (IPR) and prune them away, which gives perfect accuracy on the un-corrupted dataset. We also show that regularization has a big effect on the network's ability to memorize the corrupted examples. Weight decay, Dropout and BatchNorm all prevent memorization, but they do it differently: Weight decay and Dropout get rid of the memorizing neurons by turning them into generalizing ones, and BatchNorm de-amplifies the signal from the memorizing neurons but does not eliminate them.

steps.text:

## 1.1 Preliminaries

## Grokking modular arithmetic.

We consider the modular addition task (m+n)\,\%\,p, which can be learned by a two-layer MLP. The network function explicitly takes form

Here {\bm{e}}_{m},{\bm{e}}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} are the one_hot encoded numbers m,n. " \oplus " is concatenation of vectors ({\bm{e}}_{m}\oplus{\bm{e}}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{2p}). {\bm{W}}_{in}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 2p} is the first layer weight matrix and {\bm{W}}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times N} is the second. \phi is the activation function. {\bm{W}}_{in} is split into two N\times P blocks: {\bm{U}},{\bm{V}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times p}, which are the embedding vectors for m,n. {\bm{f}}(m,n)\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is the network-output for one example pair (m,n). The targets are the one_hot encoded answers {\bm{e}}_{(m+n)\,\%\,p}.

There are p^{2} examples pairs in the dataset; we randomly pick \alpha p^{2} of them for training and the other (1-\alpha)p^{2} examples are the test set. \alpha is called the data fraction.

This setup shows grokking, which is a delayed and sudden occurrence of generalization long after memorization.

## Periodic weights.

If we choose the quadratic activation function \phi(x)=x^{2} the problem can be solved analytically. After grokking, the trained network weights are qualitatively similar to the analytical solution from that work. The following analytical expression for the network weights gives 100\% generalization (if the width is large enough)

where \sigma(k) is a random permutation of k in S_{N}, which reflects the permutation symmetry of the hidden neurons. The phases \phi_{k}^{(u)} and \phi_{k}^{(v)} are sampled uniformly i.i.d. between (-\pi,\pi]. More details about the analytical solution are in Appendix D.

## Inverse participation ratio.

To characterize the generalizing representations quantitatively we use the inverse participation ratio (IPR), a quantity familiar from the physics of localization. It is used to detect periodicity in the weight matrix.

Let {\bm{U}}_{k\cdot},{\bm{V}}_{k\cdot}({\bm{W}}_{k\cdot}) be the k^{th} row(column) vectors of the weights {\bm{U}},{\bm{V}}({\bm{W}}). We take the discrete Fourier transforms of these vectors, \widetilde{\bm{U}}_{k\cdot},\widetilde{\bm{V}}_{k\cdot}(\widetilde{\bm{W}}_{k\cdot}). For the periodic rows(columns) of these weights the Fourier decompositions are highly localized. We use this to quantify how similar the trained weights are to the analytic solution (equation 2). So we define the Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) for these vectors:

where \lVert\cdot\rVert_{P} is the L^{P} -norm of the vector. From equation 3 we can see that IPR\in[1/p,1], and it is higher for periodic vectors and lower for non-periodic ones. It is useful to quantify the periodicity of each neuron in the hidden layer (indexed by k). We define per-neuron IPR as the average over the weight-vectors connected to the neuron:

Trained networks generalize via the periodic features, so more high-IPR neurons means better generalization. To quantify the overall similarity of the trained network to the analytical solution (equation 2) we average \text{IPR}_{k} over all hidden neurons: \overline{\text{IPR}}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{k}\left[\text{IPR}_{k}\right].

## Label corruption.

For label corruption we choose a fraction \xi of the training examples and replace their true labels with random labels. The corrupted labels come from a uniform random distribution over all the labels. In the literature this is often called symmetric label noise. This kind of label corruption does not introduce label asymmetry.

## 1.2 Related Works

## Grokking

Grokking was first reported by earlier work for Transformers trained on modular arithmetic datasets. Other work explained grokking in terms of quality of representation learning and also weight-norms, and they also found grokking-like behaviours on other datasets. Grokked Transformer models were reverse-engineered and this revealed the learned algorithm underneath. Grokking was observed on the sparse-parity problem, where it was attributed to the amplification of the so-called Fourier gap. Another study looked at grokking in the sparse-parity setup and attributed it to sparse subnetworks emerging. Solvable models for grokking in a teacher-student setup are discussed in another paper. Recently the loss landscape at early training time was investigated and used to predict when grokking occurs. And new grokking-behaviours were demonstrated by looking at the critical amount of data needed for grokking.

## Label Noise

It was shown that neural networks can easily fit random labels. A lot of work has gone into techniques for robust training with label noise: explicit regularization, noise-robust loss functions, sample selection, noise modeling and dedicated architectures etc. Recent reviews give a comprehensive overview.

## Regularization and Pruning

The interplay between label corruption and regularization in vision tasks was investigated in prior work. They showed that BatchNorm and Dropout have qualitatively different effects. Dropout effectively makes the network-size smaller but does not discourage over-reliance on a few special directions in weights space, while BatchNorm spreads the generalizing features over many dimensions. It was also found that when pruning trained networks there is a trade-off between stability and generalization.

So we define the Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) [14,15,12] for these vectors:

where \lVert\cdot\rVert_{P} is the L^{P} -norm of the vector. From equation 3 we can see that IPR\in[1/p,1], and it is higher for periodic vectors and lower for non-periodic ones. It is useful to quantify the periodicity of each neuron in the hidden layer (indexed by k). We define per-neuron IPR as the average over the weight-vectors connected to the neuron:

Trained networks generalize via the periodic features, so more high-IPR neurons means better generalization. To quantify the overall similarity of the trained network to the analytical solution (equation 2) we average \text{IPR}_{k} over all hidden neurons: \overline{\text{IPR}}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{k}\left[\text{IPR}_{k}\right].

## Label corruption.

For label corruption we choose a fraction \xi of the training examples and replace their true labels with random labels. The corrupted labels come from a uniform random distribution over all the labels. In the literature this is often called symmetric label noise [16]. This kind of label corruption does not introduce label asymmetry.

## 1.2 Related Works

## Grokking

Grokking was first reported by [13] for Transformers trained on modular arithmetic datasets. Other work [11,17] explained grokking in terms of quality of representation learning and also weight-norms, and they also found grokking-like behaviours on other datasets. Grokked Transformer models were reverse-engineered [10,18] and this revealed the learned algorithm underneath. Grokking was observed on the sparse-parity problem [19], where it was attributed to the amplification of the so-called Fourier gap. Another study [20] looked at grokking in the sparse-parity setup and attributed it to sparse subnetworks emerging. Solvable models for grokking in a teacher-student setup are discussed in [21]. Recently the loss landscape at early training time was investigated and used to predict when grokking occurs [22]. And new grokking-behaviours were demonstrated by looking at the critical amount of data needed for grokking [23].

## Label Noise

It was shown [4] that neural networks can easily fit random labels. A lot of work has gone into techniques for robust training with label noise: explicit regularization [24,25], noise-robust loss functions [26], sample selection [27,28], noise modeling and dedicated architectures [29,30,31] etc. Recent reviews [16,32] give a comprehensive overview.

## Regularization and Pruning

The interplay between label corruption and regularization in vision tasks was investigated in [33]. They showed that BatchNorm [25] and Dropout [24] have qualitatively different effects. Dropout effectively makes the network-size smaller but does not discourage over-reliance on a few special directions in weights space, while BatchNorm spreads the generalizing features over many dimensions. It was also found [34] that when pruning trained networks there is a trade-off between stability and generalization.

steps.text:
The astounding progress of deep learning in the last decade has been facilitated by massive, high-quality datasets. Annotated real-world datasets inevitably contain noisy labels, due to biases of annotation schemes [1,2] or inherent ambiguity [3]. A key challenge in training large models is therefore to prevent overfitting the noisy data and attain robust generalization performance. On the other hand, in large models it is possible for memorization and generalization to coexist [4,5]. By and large, the tussle between memorization and generalization, especially in the presence of label corruption, remains poorly understood.

In generative language models the problem of memorization is even more nuanced. On the one hand, some factual knowledge is critical for language models to produce accurate information. On the other hand, verbatim memorization of the training data is generally unwanted due to privacy concerns [6]. The full scope of the conditions that affect memorization in large language models (LLMs) is still under investigation [7,8]. In particular, larger models as well as repeated data [9] favor memorization.

In this work, we take an approach to disentangling generalization and memorization that is motivated by theoretical physics. Namely, we focus on simple, analytically tractable, ("mechanistically") interpretable models trained on algorithmic datasets. More concretely, we study two-layer Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) trained on modular arithmetic tasks, where the network is trained to learn a rule, such as z=(m+n)\%p\equiv m+n\,\,\textrm{mod}\,\,p from a number of examples. These tasks are phrased as classification problems. We then force the network to memorize \xi\cdot 100\% of the examples by corrupting the labels, i.e. injecting data points where (m+n)\%p is mapped to z^{\prime}\neq z. In this setting, the generalizing representations are understood qualitatively [10,11] as well as quantitatively, thanks to an analytic solution for the representations described in [12]. We empirically show that sufficiently large networks can memorize the corrupted examples while achieving nearly perfect generalization on the test set. The neurons responsible for memorization can be identified using inverse participation ratio (IPR) and pruned away, which leads to perfect accuracy on the un-corrupted dataset. We further show that regularization strongly affects the network's ability to memorize the corrupted examples. Weight decay, Dropout and BatchNorm all prevent memorization, but in different ways: Weight decay and Dropout eliminate the memorizing neurons by converting them into generalizing ones, while BatchNorm de-amplifies the signal coming from the memorizing neurons without eliminating them.

## 1.1 Preliminaries

## Grokking modular arithmetic.

We consider the modular addition task (m+n)\,\%\,p, which can be learned by a two-layer MLP. Explicitly, the network function takes form

Here, {\bm{e}}_{m},{\bm{e}}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} are one_hot encoded numbers m,n. " \oplus " denotes concatenation of vectors ({\bm{e}}_{m}\oplus{\bm{e}}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{2p}). {\bm{W}}_{in}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 2p} and {\bm{W}}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times N} are the first and second layer weight matrices, respectively, and \phi is the activation function. {\bm{W}}_{in} is decomposed into two N\times P blocks: {\bm{U}},{\bm{V}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times p}, which serve as embedding vectors for m,n respectively. {\bm{f}}(m,n)\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is the network-output on one example pair (m,n). The targets are one_hot encoded answers {\bm{e}}_{(m+n)\,\%\,p}.

The dataset consists of p^{2} examples pairs, from which we randomly pick \alpha p^{2} examples for training and use the other (1-\alpha)p^{2} examples as a test set. We refer to \alpha as the data fraction.

This setup exhibits grokking: a delayed and sudden occurrence of generalization, long after memorization [13,10,11,12].

## Periodic weights.

Choosing the quadratic activation function \phi(x)=x^{2} makes the problem analytically solvable [12]. Upon grokking, the trained network weights are qualitatively similar to the analytical solution presented in [12]. The following analytical expression for the network weights leads to 100\% generalization (for sufficiently large width)

## Inverse participation ratio.

To characterize the generalizing representations quantitatively, we use a quantity familiar from the physics of localization: the inverse participation ratio (IPR). Its role is to detect periodicity in the weight matrix.

Let {\bm{U}}_{k\cdot},{\bm{V}}_{k\cdot}({\bm{W}}_{k\cdot}) denote the k^{th} row(column) vectors of the weights {\bm{U}},{\bm{V}}({\bm{W}}), and consider their discrete Fourier transforms, denoted by \widetilde{\bm{U}}_{k\cdot},\widetilde{\bm{V}}_{k\cdot}(\widetilde{\bm{W}}_{k\cdot}). The Fourier decompositions of the periodic rows(columns) of these weights are highly localized. We use this to quantify the similarity of trained weights to the analytic solution (equation 2). To that end, we define the Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) [14,15,12] for these vectors:

where \lVert\cdot\rVert_{P} denotes the L^{P} -norm of the vector. From equation 3 one can see that IPR\in[1/p,1], with higher values for periodic vectors and lower values for non-periodic ones. It is useful to quantify the periodicity of each neuron in the hidden layer of the network (indexed by k), so we define per-neuron IPR by averaging over the weight-vectors connected to the neuron:

Since trained networks generalize via the periodic features, a larger population of high-IPR neurons leads to better generalization. To quantify the overall similarity of the trained network to the analytical solution (equation 2) we average \text{IPR}_{k} over all hidden neurons: \overline{\text{IPR}}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{k}\left[\text{IPR}_{k}\right].

## Label corruption.

To introduce label corruption, we choose a fraction \xi of the training examples and replace the true labels with random labels, generated from a uniform random distribution over all the labels. This is often called symmetric label noise in the literature [16]. This type of label corruption does not introduce label asymmetry.

## 1.2 Related Works

## Grokking

Grokking was first reported by [13] for Transformers trained on modular arithmetic datasets. [11,17] explained grokking in terms of the quality of representation learning as well as weight-norms, and also found grokking-like behaviours on other datasets. [10,18] reverse-engineered grokked Transformer models and revealed the underlying learned algorithm. [19] observed grokking on the sparse-parity problem and attributed it to the amplification of the so-called Fourier gap. [20] examined grokking in the sparse-parity setup and attributed it to the emergence of sparse subnetworks. [21] discuss solvable models for grokking in a teacher-student setup. Recently, [22] investigated the loss landscape at early training time and used it to predict the occurrence of grokking. [23] demonstrated new grokking-behaviours by investigating the critical amount of data needed for grokking.

## Label Noise

[4] showed that neural networks can easily fit random labels. A large body of work has developed techniques for robust training with label noise: explicit regularization [24,25], noise-robust loss functions [26], sample selection [27,28], noise modeling and dedicated architectures [29,30,31] etc. We refer the reader to recent reviews by [16,32] for a comprehensive overview.

## Regularization and Pruning

[33] investigated the interplay between label corruption and regularization in vision tasks, showing that BatchNorm [25] and Dropout [24] have qualitatively different effects. Dropout effectively reduces the network-size but does not discourage over-reliance on a few special directions in weights space, while BatchNorm spreads the generalizing features over many dimensions. [34] found a trade-off between stability and generalization when pruning trained networks.
